what: The heuristic precomputes CVRP structure from the task: customer/depot identities are discovered from loc and visited facts, distances are taken from grounded operator costs (visit, return-to-depot), and demand/capacity/vehicle-limits are read from numeric variables when available. At evaluation time it reads the current location, visited customers, current load, and used-vehicle count. It then greedily builds a sequence over all unvisited customers: from the current customer/depot it repeatedly selects the nearest remaining feasible transition, using either a direct visit when the remaining capacity allows, or a visit-via-depot transition when it must reset load and has an available vehicle. The route is closed by returning to the depot. If the remaining customers cannot be reached under the vehicle limit, a large dead-end penalty is added.
why: CVRP optimal cost is dominated by route ordering and vehicle switches. Grounded operator costs provide an exact, instance-general way to reconstruct travel costs without relying on fragile derived travel-cost names. The greedy nearest-neighbor approach respects the two crucial CVRP transition types in this PDDL domain: direct visits that accumulate load and via-depot visits that start a new vehicle and reset load. This gives a cheap but informative estimate of the remaining routing cost, including both distance and capacity/vehicle feasibility, which helps reduce search expansion without requiring admissibility.
